{{short description|Multi-dimensional object whose lengths in each dimension are similar}}

In [[geometry]], a '''fat object''' is an object in two or more dimensions, whose lengths in the different dimensions are similar. For example, a [[square]] is fat because its length and width are identical. A 2-by-1 [[rectangle]] is thinner than a square, but it is fat relative to a 10-by-1 rectangle. Similarly, a [[circle]] is fatter than a 1-by-10 [[ellipse]] and an [[equilateral triangle]] is fatter than a very [[obtuse triangle]].

Fat objects are especially important in [[computational geometry]]. Many algorithms in computational geometry can perform much better if their input consists of only fat objects; see the [[#Applications|applications]] section below.

== Global fatness ==
[[File:Two-cubes-slimness.png|thumb|right]]
Given a constant {{math|''R'' ≥ 1}}, an object {{mvar|o}} is called '''{{mvar|R}}-fat''' if its "slimness factor" is at most {{mvar|R}}. The "slimness factor" has different definitions in different papers. A common definition<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/s0925-7721(96)00027-2| title = 3-D vertical ray shooting and 2-D point enclosure, range searching, and arc shooting amidst convex fat objects| journal = [[Computational Geometry (journal)|Computational Geometry]]| volume = 8| issue = 6| pages = 299–316| year = 1997| last1 = Katz | first1 = M. J. | s2cid = 122806176| url = https://hal.inria.fr/inria-00074101/file/RR-2583.pdf}}, {{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/0925-7721(95)00005-8| title = Computing depth orders for fat objects and related problems| journal = Computational Geometry| volume = 5| issue = 4| pages = 187| year = 1995| last1 = Agarwal | first1 = P. K. | last2 = Katz | first2 = M. J. | last3 = Sharir | first3 = M. | doi-access = free}}</ref> is:

:<math>\frac{\text{side of smallest cube enclosing} \ o}{\text{side of largest cube enclosed in} \ o}</math>

where {{mvar|o}} and the [[cube]]s are {{mvar|d}}-dimensional. A 2-dimensional cube is a [[square]], so the slimness factor of a square is 1 (since its smallest enclosing square is the same as its largest enclosed disk). The slimness factor of a 10-by-1 rectangle is 10. The slimness factor of a circle is √2. Hence, by this definition, a square is 1-fat but a disk and a 10×1 rectangle are not 1-fat. A square is also 2-fat (since its slimness factor is less than 2), 3-fat, etc. A disk is also 2-fat (and also 3-fat etc.), but a 10×1 rectangle is not 2-fat. Every shape is ∞-fat, since by definition the slimness factor is always at most ∞.

The above definition can be termed '''two-cubes''' fatness since it is based on the ratio between the side-lengths of two cubes. Similarly, it is possible to define '''two-balls''' fatness, in which a [[Ball (mathematics)|d-dimensional ball]] is used instead.<ref name=EfratEtAl2000>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/s0925-7721(99)00059-0| title = Dynamic data structures for fat objects and their applications| journal = Computational Geometry| volume = 15| issue = 4| pages = 215| year = 2000| last1 = Efrat | first1 = A. | last2 = Katz | first2 = M. J. | last3 = Nielsen | first3 = F. | last4 = Sharir | first4 = M. | doi-access = free }}</ref> A 2-dimensional ball is a [[Disk (mathematics)|disk]]. According to this alternative definition, a disk is 1-fat but a square is not 1-fat, since its two-balls-slimness is √2.

An alternative definition, that can be termed '''enclosing-ball''' fatness (also called "thickness"<ref name=vanderStappenEtAl1993>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/0925-7721(93)90007-s| title = The complexity of the free space for a robot moving amidst fat obstacles| journal = Computational Geometry| volume = 3| issue = 6| pages = 353| year = 1993| last1 = Van Der Stappen | first1 = A. F. | last2 = Halperin | first2 = D. | last3 = Overmars | first3 = M. H. | hdl = 1874/16650| hdl-access = free}}</ref>) is based on the following slimness factor:

:<math>\left(\frac{\text{volume of smallest ball enclosing} \ o}{\text{volume of} \ o}\right)^{1/d}</math>

The exponent {{math|{{sfrac|1|''d''}}}} makes this definition a ratio of two lengths, so that it is comparable to the two-balls-fatness.

Here, too, a cube can be used instead of a ball.

Similarly it is possible to define the '''enclosed-ball''' fatness based on the following slimness factor:

:<math>\left(\frac{\text{volume of} \ o}{\text{volume of largest  ball enclosed in} \ o}\right)^{1/d}</math>

=== Enclosing-fatness vs. enclosed-fatness ===

The enclosing-ball/cube-slimness might be very different from the enclosed-ball/cube-slimness.

For example, consider a [[lollipop]] with a candy in the shape of a {{math|1 × 1}} square and a stick in the shape of a {{math|''b'' × {{sfrac|1|''b''}}}} rectangle (with {{math|''b'' > 1 > {{sfrac|1|''b''}}}}). As {{mvar|b}} increases, the area of the enclosing cube ({{math|≈ ''b''<sup>2</sup>}}) increases, but the area of the enclosed cube remains constant (=1) and the total area of the shape also remains constant (=2). Thus the enclosing-cube-slimness can grow arbitrarily while the enclosed-cube-slimness remains constant (=√2). See this [https://www.geogebra.org/m/Sdh2y2pG GeoGebra page] for a demonstration.

On the other hand, consider a rectilinear 'snake' with width {{math|{{sfrac|1|''b''}}}} and length {{mvar|b}}, that is entirely folded within a square of side length 1. As {{mvar|b}} increases, the area of the enclosed cube ({{math|≈ {{sfrac|1|''b''<sup>2</sup>}}}}) decreases, but the total areas of the snake and of the enclosing cube remain constant (=1). Thus the enclosed-cube-slimness can grow arbitrarily while the enclosing-cube-slimness remains constant (=1).

With both the lollipop and the snake, the two-cubes-slimness grows arbitrarily, since in general:

<math display=block>
  \left({\text{enclosing-ball-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \times \left({\text{enclosed-ball-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) = \left({\text{two-balls-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right)
</math>
<math display=block>
  \left({\text{enclosing-cube-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \times \left({\text{enclosed-cube-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) = \left({\text{two-cubes-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right)
</math>

Since all slimness factor are at least 1, it follows that if an object {{mvar|o}} is {{mvar|R}}-fat according to the two-balls/cubes definition, it is also {{mvar|R}}-fat according to the enclosing-ball/cube and enclosed-ball/cube definitions (but the opposite is not true, as exemplified above).

=== Balls vs. cubes ===
[[Volume of an n-ball|The volume]] of a {{mvar|d}}-dimensional ball of radius {{mvar|r}} is: <math>V_d\cdot r^d,</math> where {{mvar|V<sub>d</sub>}} is a dimension-dependent constant:
<math display=block>
  V_d = \frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma \left(\frac{d}{2} + 1 \right)}
</math>

A {{mvar|d}}-dimensional cube with side-length {{math|2''a''}} has volume {{math|(2''a'')<sup>''d''</sup>}}. It is enclosed in a {{mvar|d}}-dimensional ball with radius <math>a\sqrt d</math> whose volume is <math>V_d \left(a\sqrt d \right)^d.</math> Hence for every {{mvar|d}}-dimensional object:

<math display=block>
  \left({\text{enclosing-ball-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \leq \left({\text{enclosing-cube-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \times \sqrt[d]{V_d} \times \frac{\sqrt d}{2}</math>

For even dimensions ({{math|1=''d'' = 2''k''}}), the factor simplifies to: <math>\sqrt\tfrac{\pi k}{2} \left/ \sqrt[2k]{k!} \right. .</math> In particular, for two-dimensional shapes {{math|1=''V''<sub>2</sub> = π}} and the factor is: <math>\sqrt{\tfrac{\pi}{2}} \approx 1.25,</math> so:

<math display=block>
  \left({\text{enclosing-disk-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \leq \left({\text{enclosing-square-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \times 1.25
</math>

From similar considerations:

<math display=block>
  \left({\text{enclosed-cube-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \leq \left({\text{enclosed-ball-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \times \sqrt[d]{V_d} \times \frac{\sqrt d}{2}</math>
<math display=block>
  \left({\text{enclosed-square-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \leq \left({\text{enclosed-disk-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \times 1.25</math>

A {{mvar|d}}-dimensional ball with radius {{mvar|a}} is enclosed in a {{mvar|d}}-dimensional cube with side-length {{math|2''a''}}. Hence for every {{mvar|d}}-dimensional object:

<math display=block>
  \left({\text{enclosing-cube-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \leq \left({\text{enclosing-ball-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \times \frac{2}{\sqrt[d]{V_d}}</math>

For even dimensions ({{math|1=''d'' = 2''k''}}), the factor simplifies to: <math display=inline>2 \left/ \sqrt[2k]{(k!)} \ \right/ \sqrt\pi.</math> In particular, for two-dimensional shapes the factor is: <math>\tfrac{2}{\sqrt\pi} \approx 1.13,</math> so:

<math display=block>
  \left({\text{enclosing-square-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \leq \left({\text{enclosing-disk-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \times 1.13</math>

From similar considerations:

<math display=block>
  \left({\text{enclosed-ball-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \leq \left({\text{enclosed-cube-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \times \frac{2}{\sqrt[d]{V_d}}</math>
<math display=block>
  \left({\text{enclosed-disk-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \leq \left({\text{enclosed-square-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \times 1.13</math>

Multiplying the above relations gives the following simple relations:

<math display=block>
  \left({\text{two-balls-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \leq \left({\text{two-cubes-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \times \sqrt{d}</math>
<math display=block>
  \left({\text{two-cubes-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \leq \left({\text{two-balls-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \times \sqrt{d}</math>

Thus, an {{mvar|R}}-fat object according to the either the two-balls or the two-cubes definition is at most {{tmath|R\sqrt d}}-fat according to the alternative definition.

== Local fatness ==

The above definitions are all ''global'' in the sense that they don't care about small thin areas that are part of a large fat object.

For example, consider a [[lollipop]] with a candy in the shape of a {{math|1 × 1}} square and a stick in the shape of a {{math|1 × {{sfrac|1|''b''}}}} rectangle (with {{math|''b'' > 1 > {{sfrac|1|''b''}}}}). As {{mvar|b}} increases, the area of the enclosing cube (=4) and the area of the enclosed cube (=1) remain constant, while the total area of the shape changes only slightly ({{math|1== 1 + {{sfrac|1|''b''}}}}). Thus all three slimness factors are bounded: 

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  \left({\text{enclosing-cube-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) &\leq 2, \\[4pt]
  \left({\text{enclosed-cube-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) &\leq 2, \\[4pt]
  \left({\text{two-cube-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) &= 2.
\end{align}</math>

Thus by all definitions the lollipop is 2-fat. However, the stick-part of the lollipop obviously becomes thinner and thinner.

In some applications, such thin parts are unacceptable, so '''local fatness''', based on a local slimness factor, may be more appropriate. For every global slimness factor, it is possible to define a local version. For example, for the enclosing-ball-slimness, it is possible to define the '''local-enclosing-ball''' slimness factor of an object {{mvar|o}} by considering the set {{mvar|B}} of all balls whose center is inside {{mvar|o}} and whose boundary intersects the boundary of {{mvar|o}} (i.e. not entirely containing {{mvar|o}}). The local-enclosing-ball-slimness factor is defined as:<ref name=vanderStappenEtAl1993 /><ref>{{Cite book | doi = 10.1007/3-540-58218-5_6| chapter = New results on binary space partitions in the plane (extended abstract)| title = Algorithm Theory — SWAT '94| volume = 824| pages = 61| series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science| year = 1994| last1 = Berg | first1 = M. | last2 = Groot | first2 = M. | last3 = Overmars | first3 = M. | isbn = 978-3-540-58218-2}}, {{Cite book| doi = 10.1145/177424.177453| chapter = Motion planning amidst fat obstacles (extended abstract)| title = Proceedings of the tenth annual symposium on Computational geometry - SCG '94| pages = 31| year = 1994| last1 = Van Der Stappen | first1 = A. F. | last2 = Overmars | first2 = M. H. | isbn = 978-0897916486| s2cid = 152761}}, {{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/0020-0190(92)90211-d| title = Point location in fat subdivisions| journal = Information Processing Letters| volume = 44| issue = 5| pages = 261–265| year = 1992| last1 = Overmars | first1 = M. H. | type = Submitted manuscript| hdl = 1874/17965| hdl-access = free}}, {{Cite journal | doi = 10.1006/jagm.1996.0063| title = Range Searching and Point Location among Fat Objects| journal = Journal of Algorithms| volume = 21| issue = 3| pages = 629| year = 1996| last1 = Overmars | first1 = M. H. | last2 = Van Der Stappen | first2 = F. A. | hdl = 1874/17327| hdl-access = free}}</ref>

<math display=block>
  \frac{1}{2}\cdot \sup_{b \in B}\left(\frac{\text{volume} (B)}{\text{volume} (B\cap o)}\right)^{1/d}
</math>

The 1/2 is a normalization factor that makes the local-enclosing-ball-slimness of a ball equal to 1. The local-enclosing-ball-slimness of the lollipop-shape described above is dominated by the {{math|1 × {{sfrac|1|''b''}}}} stick, and it goes to ∞ as {{mvar|b}} grows. Thus by the local definition the above lollipop is not 2-fat.

=== Global vs. local definitions ===

Local-fatness implies global-fatness. Here is a proof sketch for fatness based on enclosing balls. By definition, the volume of the smallest enclosing ball is ≤ the volume of any other enclosing ball. In particular, it is ≤ the volume of any enclosing ball whose center is inside {{mvar|o}} and whose boundary touches the boundary of {{mvar|o}}. But every such enclosing ball {{mvar|b}} is in the set {{mvar|B}} considered by the definition of local-enclosing-ball slimness. Hence:

<math display=block>\begin{align}
  \left({\text{enclosing-ball-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right)^d
  &= \frac{\text{volume(smallest enclosing ball)}}{\text{volume}(o)} \\[4pt]
  &\leq \frac{\text{volume} (b \in B)}{\text{volume}(o)} \\[4pt]
  &= \frac{\text{volume} (b \in B)}{\text{volume}(b \cap o)} \\[4pt]
  &\leq \left[ 2 \times \left({\text{local-enclosing-} \atop \text{ball-slimness}}\right) \right]^d
\end{align}</math>

Hence:

<math display=block>
  \left({\text{enclosing-ball-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right) \leq \left({\text{local-enclosing-} \atop \text{ball-slimness}}\right) \times 2
</math>

For a [[convex body]], the opposite is also true: local-fatness implies global-fatness. The proof<ref name=vanderStappenEtAl1993/> is based on the following lemma. Let {{mvar|o}} be a convex object. Let {{mvar|P}} be a point in {{mvar|o}}. Let {{mvar|b}} and {{mvar|B}} be two balls centered at {{mvar|P}} such that {{mvar|b}} is smaller than {{mvar|B}}. Then {{mvar|o}} intersects a larger portion of {{mvar|b}} than of {{mvar|B}}, i.e.:

<math display=block>
  \frac{\text{volume} \ (b \cap o)}{\text{volume} \ (b)} \geq \frac{\text{volume} \ (B \cap o)}{\text{volume} \ (B)}
</math>

Proof sketch: standing at the point {{mvar|P}}, we can look at different angles {{mvar|θ}} and measure the distance to the boundary of {{mvar|o}}. Because {{mvar|o}} is convex, this distance is a function, say {{math|''r''(''θ'')}}. We can calculate the left-hand side of the inequality by integrating the following function (multiplied by some determinant function) over all angles:
<math display=block>
  f(\theta) = \min{\left(\frac{r(\theta)}{\text{radius} \ (b)},1 \right)}
</math>

Similarly we can calculate the right-hand side of the inequality by integrating the following function:
<math display=block>
  F(\theta) = \min{ \left(\frac{r(\theta)}{\text{radius} \ (B)},1 \right)}
</math>

By checking all 3 possible cases, it is possible to show that always {{math|''f''(''&theta;'') &ge; ''F''(''&theta;'')}}. Thus the integral of {{mvar|f}} is at least the integral of {{mvar|F}}, and the lemma follows.

The definition of local-enclosing-ball slimness considers ''all'' balls that are centered in a point in {{mvar|o}} and intersect the boundary of {{mvar|o}}. However, when {{mvar|o}} is convex, the above lemma allows us to consider, for each point in {{mvar|o}}, only balls that are maximal in size, i.e., only balls that entirely contain {{mvar|o}} (and whose boundary intersects the boundary of {{mvar|o}}). For every such ball {{mvar|b}}:

<math display=block>
  \text{volume} \ (b)\leq C_d\cdot \text{diameter} \ (o)^d
</math>

where {{mvar|C{{sub|d}}}} is some dimension-dependent constant.

The diameter of {{mvar|o}} is at most the diameter of the smallest ball enclosing {{mvar|o}}, and the volume of that ball is: 
<math display=block>C_d \cdot \left( \frac{\text{diameter(smallest ball enclosing}\ o)}{2} \right)^d
</math> 

Combining all inequalities gives that for every ''convex'' object:

<math display=block>
  \left({\text{local-enclosing-} \atop \text{ball-slimness}}\right) \leq \left({\text{enclosing-ball-} \atop \text{slimness}}\right)
</math>

For non-convex objects, this inequality of course doesn't hold, as exemplified by the lollipop above.

== Fatness of a triangle ==

Slimness is invariant to scale, so the slimness factor of a triangle (as of any other polygon) can be presented as a function of its angles only. The three ball-based slimness factors can be calculated using well-known trigonometric identities.

=== Enclosed-ball slimness ===
The largest circle contained in a triangle is called its [[incircle]]. It is [[Incircle and excircles of a triangle#Relation to area of the triangle|known]] that:

<math display=block> \Delta = r^2 \cdot \left(\cot \frac{\angle A}{2} + \cot \frac{\angle B}{2} + \cot \frac{\angle C}{2} \right)</math>

where {{math|Δ}} is the area of a triangle and {{mvar|r}} is the radius of the incircle. Hence, the enclosed-ball slimness of a triangle is:

<math display=block>\sqrt{ \frac{\cot \frac{\angle A}{2} + \cot \frac{\angle B}{2} + \cot \frac{\angle C}{2}}{\pi} }</math>

=== Enclosing-ball slimness ===

The smallest containing circle for an [[acute triangle]] is its [[circumcircle]], while for an [[obtuse triangle]] it is the circle having the triangle's longest side as a diameter.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Rajan | first = V. T.
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02574375
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Discrete & Computational Geometry]]
 | mr = 1283887
 | pages = 189–202
 | title = Optimality of the Delaunay triangulation in <math>\R^d</math>
 | volume = 12
 | year = 1994| doi-access = free
 }}</ref>

It is [[Circumscribed circle#Triangles|known]] that:

<math display=block>\Delta = R^2 \cdot 2 \sin A \sin B \sin C</math>

where again {{math|Δ}} is the area of a triangle and {{mvar|R}} is the radius of the circumcircle. Hence, for an acute triangle, the enclosing-ball slimness factor is:

<math display=block>\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2 \sin A \sin B \sin C}}</math>

It is also [[Triangle#Using trigonometry|known]] that:

<math display=block>
  \Delta = \frac{c^{2}}{2(\cot \angle{A} + \cot \angle{B})} 
  = \frac{c^{2}(\sin \angle{A})(\sin \angle{B})}{2\sin(\angle{A} + \angle{B})}</math>

where {{mvar|c}} is any side of the triangle and {{math|''A'', ''B''}} are the adjacent angles. Hence, for an obtuse triangle with acute angles {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}} (and longest side {{mvar|c}}), the enclosing-ball slimness factor is:

<math display=block>
  \sqrt{\frac{\pi\cdot(\cot \angle{A} + \cot \angle{B})}{2}} 
  = \sqrt{\frac{\pi\cdot\sin(\angle{A} + \angle{B})}{2 (\sin \angle{A}) (\sin \angle{B})}}
</math>

Note that in a [[right triangle]], <math>\sin{\angle{C}} = \sin(\angle{A} + \angle{B}) = 1,</math> so the two expressions coincide.

=== Two-balls slimness ===

The inradius {{mvar|r}} and the circumradius {{mvar|R}} are connected via a couple of formulae which provide two alternative expressions for the two-balls slimness of an acute triangle:<ref>{{cite web|last1=Weisstein|first1=Eric W|title=Inradius|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/Inradius.html|website=MathWorld|accessdate=28 September 2014}}</ref>

<math display=block>
  \frac{R}{r} = \frac{1}{4 \sin\frac{\angle{A}}{2} \sin\frac{\angle{B}}{2} \sin\frac{\angle{C}}{2} } 
  = \frac{1}{\cos \angle{A}  + \cos \angle{B}  + \cos \angle{C} - 1}
</math>

For an obtuse triangle, {{math|''c''/2}} should be used instead of {{mvar|R}}. By the [[law of sines]]:

<math display=block>\frac{c}{2} = R \sin{\angle{C}}</math>

Hence the slimness factor of an obtuse triangle with obtuse angle {{mvar|C}} is:

<math display=block>
  \frac{c/2}{r} = \frac{\sin{\angle{C}}}{4 \sin\frac{\angle{A}}{2} \sin\frac{\angle{B}}{2} \sin\frac{\angle{C}}{2} } 
  = \frac{\sin{\angle{C}}}{\cos\angle{A}  + \cos\angle{B}  + \cos\angle{C} - 1}
</math>

Note that in a [[right triangle]], <math>\sin{\angle{C}} = 1,</math> so the two expressions coincide.

The two expressions can be combined in the following way to get a single expression for the two-balls slimness of any triangle with smaller angles {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}:

<math display=block>
  \frac{\sin{\max(\angle{A}, \angle{B}, \angle{C}, \pi/2)}}{4 \sin\frac{\angle{A}}{2} \sin\frac{\angle{B}}{2} \sin\frac{\pi - \angle{A} - \angle{B}}{2} } 
  = \frac{\sin{\max(\angle{A}, \angle{B}, \angle{C}, \pi/2)}}{\cos\angle{A} + \cos\angle{B} - \cos (\angle{A} + \angle{B}) - 1}
</math>

To get a feeling of the rate of change in fatness, consider what this formula gives for an [[isosceles triangle]] with head angle {{mvar|θ}} [[Small-angle approximation|when {{mvar|θ}} is small]]:
<math display=block>
  \frac{\sin{\max(\theta, \pi/2)}}{4 \sin^2\frac{\pi - \theta}{4} \sin\frac{\theta}{2}} \approx \frac{1}{4 {\sqrt{1/2}}^2 \theta/2} = \frac{1}{\theta}
</math>

<!--van der Stappen et al. give the following formula for the enclosing-ball slimness: (√(π/tan''θ'')<ref name=vanderStappenEtAl1993/>) -->

The following graphs show the 2-balls slimness factor of a triangle:
* Slimness of a general triangle [https://www.desmos.com/calculator/zsn0i0hvmr when one angle (''a'') is a constant parameter while the other angle (''x'') changes].
* Slimness of an isosceles triangle [https://www.desmos.com/calculator/rkpz7pscra as a function of its head angle (''x'')].
<!--
=== Cube-based slimness ===
The cube-based slimness of a triangle is much more difficult to calculate than its ball-based slimness.  It can be calculated for an [[isosceles triangle]] with base angles ''θ''.
* When 60°≤''θ''≤arctan(2)=63.5°: enclosing-cube = 2/(√tan''θ''), enclosed-cube = (√tan''θ'')/2+(1/√tan''θ''), two-cubes = 1+2/tan''θ''.
* When arctan(2)=63.5°≤''θ''<90°: two-cubes = 1+tan''θ''/2.
-->

== Fatness of circles, ellipses and their parts ==
The ball-based slimness of a circle is of course 1 - the smallest possible value.

[[File:Circularsegment.svg|right|150px]]
For a [[circular segment]] with central angle {{mvar|θ}}, the circumcircle diameter is the length of the chord and the incircle diameter is the height of the segment, so the two-balls slimness (and its approximation [[Small-angle approximation|when {{mvar|θ}} is small]]) is:
<math display=block>
  \frac{\text{length of chord}}{\text{height of segment}}
  = \frac{2R\sin\frac{\theta}{2}}{R\left(1 - \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}
  = \frac{2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}}{\left(1 - \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\right)} 
  \approx \frac{\theta}{\theta^2/8} 
  = \frac{8}{\theta}</math>

[[Image:Circle arc.svg|right|150px]]
For a [[circular sector]] with central angle {{mvar|θ}} (when {{mvar|θ}} is small), the circumcircle diameter is the radius of the circle and the incircle diameter is the chord length, so the two-balls slimness is:
<math display=block>
  \frac{\text{radius of circle}}{\text{length of chord}}
  = \frac{R}{2R\sin\frac{\theta}{2}} 
  = \frac{1}{2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}} 
  \approx \frac{1}{2 \theta / 2} 
  = \frac{1}{\theta}
</math>

For an [[ellipse]], the slimness factors are different in different locations. For example, consider an ellipse with short axis {{mvar|a}} and long axis {{mvar|b}}. the length of a chord ranges between <math>2a\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}</math> at the narrow side of the ellipse and <math>2b\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}</math> at its wide side; similarly, the height of the segment ranges between <math>b\bigl(1 - \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}\bigr)</math> at the narrow side and <math>a\bigl(1 - \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}\bigr)</math> at its wide side. So the two-balls slimness ranges between:
<math display=block>
  \frac{2a\sin\frac{\theta}{2}}{b\left(1-\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\right)} \approx \frac{8a}{b\theta}
</math>

and:
<math display=block>
  \frac{2b\sin\frac{\theta}{2}}{a\left(1-\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\right)} \approx \frac{8b}{a\theta}
</math>

In general, when the secant starts at angle Θ the slimness factor can be approximated by:<ref>See graph at: https://www.desmos.com/calculator/fhfqju02sn</ref>

<math>\frac{2\sin\frac{\theta}{2}}{\left(1-\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}</math> <math>\left(\frac{b}{a}\cos^2(\Theta+\frac{\theta}{2}) + \frac{a}{b}\sin^2(\Theta+\frac{\theta}{2})\right)</math>

== Fatness of a convex polygon ==
A [[convex polygon]] is called '''{{mvar|r}}-separated ''' if the angle between each pair of edges (not necessarily adjacent) is at least {{mvar|r}}.

Lemma: The enclosing-ball-slimness of an {{mvar|r}}-separated convex polygon is at most <math>O(1/r)</math>.<ref name="bos13">{{cite journal|doi=10.20382/jocg.v4i1a9|arxiv=1009.1866|author1=Mark de Berg|title=Fat Polygonal Partitions with Applications to Visualization and Embeddings|journal=Journal of Computational Geometry|volume=4|last2=Onak|first2=Krzysztof|last3=Sidiropoulos|first3=Anastasios|year=2010|s2cid=15245776}}</ref>{{rp|7–8}}

A convex polygon is called '''{{math|''k'',''r''}}-separated ''' if:
# It does not have parallel edges, except maybe two horizontal and two vertical.
# Each non-axis-parallel edge makes an angle of at least {{mvar|r}} with any other edge, and with the {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}} axes.
# If there are two horizontal edges, then diameter/height is at most {{mvar|k}}.
# If there are two vertical edges, then diameter/width is at most {{mvar|k}}.

Lemma: The enclosing-ball-slimness of a {{math|''k'',''r''}}-separated convex polygon is at most <math>O(\max(k,1/r))</math>.<ref name="dsv2">{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.comgeo.2013.12.008|arxiv=1012.1749|title=Treemaps with bounded aspect ratio|journal=Computational Geometry|volume=47|issue=6|pages=683|year=2014|last1=De Berg|first1=Mark|last2=Speckmann|first2=Bettina|author2-link=Bettina Speckmann|last3=Van Der Weele|first3=Vincent|s2cid=12973376}}. Conference version: {{cite conference|url=http://alexandria.tue.nl/openaccess/Metis253577.pdf|title=Convex Treemaps with Bounded Aspect Ratio|conference=EuroCG|year=2011}}</ref> improve the upper bound to <math>O(d)</math>.

== Counting fat objects ==
If an object {{mvar|o}} has diameter {{math|2''a''}}, then every ball enclosing {{mvar|o}} must have radius at least {{mvar|a}} and volume at least <math>V_d a^.</math> Hence, by definition of enclosing-ball-fatness, the volume of an {{mvar|R}}-fat object with diameter {{math|2''a''}} must be at least <math>\tfrac{V_d a^d}{R^d}.</math> Hence:

:'''Lemma 1''': Let {{math|''R'' ≥ 1}} and {{math|''C'' ≥ 0}} be two constants. Consider a collection of non-overlapping {{mvar|d}}-dimensional objects that are all globally {{mvar|R}}-fat  (i.e. with enclosing-ball-slimness&nbsp;{{math|≤ ''R''}}). The number of such objects of diameter at least {{math|2''a''}}, contained in a ball of radius {{mvar|C⋅a}}, is at most: 
<math display=block>
  V_d \cdot \frac{(C a)^d }{V_d \cdot \frac{a^d}{R^d}} = (R C)^d
</math>

For example (taking {{math|1=''d'' = 2}}, {{math|1=''R'' = 1}} and {{math|1=''C'' = 3}}): The number of non-overlapping disks with radius at least 1 contained in a circle of radius 3 is at most {{math|1=3<sup>2</sup> = 9}}. (Actually, it is at most 7).

If we consider local-fatness instead of global-fatness, we can get a stronger lemma:<ref name=vanderStappenEtAl1993/>

:'''Lemma 2''': Let {{math|''R'' ≥ 1}} and {{math|''C'' ≥ 0}} be two constants. Consider a collection of non-overlapping {{mvar|d}}-dimensional objects that are all locally {{mvar|R}}-fat (i.e. with local-enclosing-ball-slimness&nbsp;{{math|≤ ''R''}}). Let {{mvar|o}} be a single object in that collection with diameter {{math|2''a''}}. Then the number of objects in the collection with diameter larger than {{math|2''a''}} that lie within distance {{math|2''C⋅a''}} from object {{mvar|o}} is at most:
<math display=block>(4 R \cdot (C+1))^d</math>

For example (taking {{math|1=''d'' = 2}}, {{math|1=''R'' = 1}} and {{math|1=''C'' = 0}}): the number of non-overlapping disks with  radius larger than 1 that touch a given [[unit disk]] is at most {{math|1=4<sup>2</sup> = 16}} (this is not a tight bound since in this case it is easy to prove an upper bound of 5).

== Generalizations ==
The following generalization of fatness were studied by <ref name=EfratEtAl2000 /> for 2-dimensional objects.

A triangle {{math|∆}} is a {{math|(''β'', ''δ'')}}-triangle of a planar object {{mvar|o}} ({{math|0 < ''β'' ≤ π/3}}, {{math|0 < ''δ'' < 1}}), if {{math|∆ ⊆ ''o''}}, each of the angles of {{math|∆}} is at least {{mvar|β}}, and the length of each of its edges is at least {{math|''δ''·diameter(''o'')}}.  An object {{mvar|o}} in the plane is '''{{math|(''β'', ''δ'')}}-covered''' if for each point {{math|''P'' ∈ ''o''}} there exists a {{math|(''β'', ''δ'')}}-triangle {{math|∆}} of {{mvar|o}} that contains {{mvar|P}}.

For [[convex body|convex objects]], the two definitions are equivalent, in the sense that if {{mvar|o}} is {{mvar|α}}-fat, for some constant {{mvar|α}}, then it is also {{math|(''β'', ''δ'')}}-covered, for appropriate constants {{mvar|β}} and {{mvar|δ}}, and vice versa. However, for non-convex objects the definition of being fat is more general than the definition of being {{math|(''β'', ''δ'')}}-covered.<ref name=EfratEtAl2000 />

== Applications ==
Fat objects are used in various problems, for example:
* [[Motion planning]] - planning a path for a robot moving amidst obstacles becomes easier when the obstacles are fat objects.<ref name=vanderStappenEtAl1993/>
* [[Fair cake-cutting]] - dividing a cake becomes more difficult when the pieces have to be fat objects. This requirement is common, for example, when the "cake" to be divided is a land-estate.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/j.jmateco.2017.01.007|title=Fair and square: Cake-cutting in two dimensions|journal=Journal of Mathematical Economics|volume=70|pages=1–28|year=2017|last1=Segal-Halevi|first1=Erel|last2=Nitzan|first2=Shmuel|last3=Hassidim|first3=Avinatan|last4=Aumann|first4=Yonatan|arxiv=1409.4511|s2cid=1278209}}</ref>
* More applications can be found in the references below.
